overview.text: Boyle’s law describes how pressure and volume change for a fixed amount of gas when temperature stays constant: increase the pressure and the volume decreases, and vice versa. Its defining feature is an inverse relationship, expressed as PV = constant; between two states, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. The law is named for Robert Boyle, the seventeenth-century natural philosopher whose work on gases helped establish the relationship experimentally. It is one of several gas laws that combine into the ideal gas law, PV = nRT. Breathing offers a familiar example: as the chest expands, lung pressure falls and air flows inward.

key_facts.text: The inverse relationship applies when both the gas’s temperature and amount remain constant.
At fixed temperature and amount, pressure multiplied by volume stays constant: PV = constant.
For two conditions of the same gas sample, the relationship can be written P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
OpenStax identifies Boyle’s law as one of four gas relationships combined in the ideal gas law, PV = nRT.
The Science Museum Group identifies Robert Boyle as an Irish natural philosopher and chemist (1627–1691), and notes that he and Robert Hooke devised an air-pump.
During inhalation, expanding the chest increases lung volume and lowers lung pressure, drawing air in—a familiar application of Boyle’s law.
